title: AI writing's moat isn't the model, it's the proprietary data you feed it
dek: Over two years, the writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during a layoff into a one-person content company and a compounding editor; the core method isn't prompts, it's using proprietary experience to cover the "last mile" the model can't reach.
why: Not a tool review, but how a non-technical writer uses AI as a mode of production: the substance is concentrated in the last 30 minutes, and the personal story up front provides the motivational context.
who: Independent writers and content entrepreneurs struggling with the quality of AI-generated writing, and anyone who wants an AI agent to take over life and administrative tasks.
skip: The layoff story and the ad break in the first few minutes can be fast-forwarded; start on the methodology at the 8:26 delivery case.

points.h: The biggest value of an AI coach isn't saving money
points.body: After being laid off she was at a low point and couldn't afford a human career coach's hourly rate, but a $20-a-month ChatGPT subscription was acceptable. She found that writing out her thoughts and letting AI question and push back from the outside helped her externalise her thinking, fight catastrophising, and gave her a sense of accountability. The most important legacy of that experience wasn't the money saved, but that it made her believe AI really can drive concrete change in a life. At the time she was wavering over whether to take Every's freelance offer, and it was ChatGPT that gave her the push to just try it.

points.h: Throughput comes from upfront context, not clever prompts
points.body: She once took on a delivery load of 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts and 16 Instagram posts in a week and a half. She could do it not because she knew a cleverer one-sentence prompt, but because she did a lot of upfront context engineering: feeding the model brand information, product details, audience profiles and differentiators all at once. Much of the demand was essentially content repurposing, and AI is good at rewriting one long piece into versions for different platforms. The rule she distilled: set the scene well up front, and only then can you move fast later.

points.h: Give the model a fence first, then talk tone and word choice
points.body: Before Claude Projects existed, she could only keep persistent documents in Google Docs and manually copy-paste them into context each time. This structure didn't fall from the sky; it comes from the style guide tradition in content marketing: first define who the audience is, what the pain points are, how the product maps to them, who the competitors are and where the differentiators lie. She says this amounts to giving the model a playground with a fence: first make sure it won't wander off, then talk about word choice, tone and reading difficulty. Later, as soon as Projects launched, she built a separate project for every client and every column.

points.h: AI writing's last mile can only be covered by a human
points.body: She believes there is a "last mile" problem in AI writing: models have a knowledge cutoff, and they aren't in the real physical world. So the human's job is to supply the latest data and real experience that AI can't reach. She warns that if you just throw the model a single line like "write a blog post about style guides", all you'll get is the generic content it already knows, which is commoditised information; what really makes writing unique is fresh ingredients the model has never seen, like internal company research, third-party reports and personal experience. The writing system is the kitchen; the human is responsible for supplying good ingredients.

points.h: AI's value is reducing friction, not speeding up output
points.body: She talks openly about her bipolar disorder and points out that AI's value isn't just producing content faster, but reducing friction in life. She put off booking a primary care doctor for three years, and eventually just had Codex find doctors who accept her insurance and are taking new patients and complete the booking; email is first filtered by automation, and only messages that genuinely need a human reply reach her inbox. She says this completely solved her email anxiety. This isn't treating AI as a production tool, but as assistive technology that makes her day-to-day running "as a person" easier.

points.h: Let AI interview you repeatedly, and it can prioritise for you
points.body: Two years ago she just asked ChatGPT whether it could be her career coach; today that coach lives in a Codex project containing her role profile, Every's brand positioning, content performance data, a folder of reader praise and her OKRs. She doesn't maintain the board herself; she uses voice conversation to have the system prioritise by highest impact, and the system also maintains her Kanban for her. The key to building this system is letting AI interview her repeatedly, then sedimenting the interview content into context. She says it's like having a Chief of Staff, not just a writer.

points.h: Feedback that only fixes the current draft is wasted
points.body: The core of the Compound Writing plugin is compounding thinking: every piece of feedback given to AI should flow back into the system so the next output is automatically better. She forked Kieran Klassen's Compound Engineering plugin and adapted it into a writing workflow: code and writing both have brainstorming, planning, drafting and review stages, except writing focuses more on structure, voice and evidence. Editing is further split into a substantive edit that looks at big structure and argument, a line edit that works sentence by sentence, and a final pass that checks before publication. Now she doesn't write in a web chat window, but pours the day's fresh material into this system.

points.h: Vonnegut as editor gives you a perspective, not a verdict
points.body: She built Vonnegut's eight narrative elements, Hitchcock's principle of suspense about the bomb under the table, and the expressive styles of Sorkin and Sedaris into the plugin as editing skills. Vonnegut checks whether "the story starts as close to the end as possible" and whether "every sentence earns its place"; Hitchcock's perspective asks whether the reader will want to keep reading because of this. She stresses that this isn't letting the masters' ghosts mark up your draft, but giving you a new perspective you can accept or reject; non-professional writers may actually benefit more, because they're less likely to be picking at themselves while they write.

points.h: AI's compounding may only compound for the few who got in early
points.body: She says her core thesis about AI today is this: access to education and to usage will matter more than ever. She lives in Columbus, Ohio, and has never lived in New York or San Francisco, which makes her care more about how opportunity is distributed. She admits she got where she is because she had financial slack, a time budget and a network that put her in touch with excellent peers; she hopes the AI community will actively create conditions so that more places and more kinds of people can get on board too. Because she sees clearly that AI has enormous compounding effects, and the cost is that the returns may only compound for the few who happened to get in early.

terms.def: Pre-organising information like brand, audience, product and differentiators into a fixed background so every AI conversation heads in the right direction.
Model training has a knowledge cutoff, so humans need to supply the latest data and real-world experience for writing not to fall into generic platitudes.
Sedimenting one-off feedback given to AI into the system so the same good decisions automatically take effect again and again in future.
Having an AI agent handle administrative chores you keep putting off, like booking doctors, filing insurance claims and clearing your inbox.

quotes.text: Clarity, it turns out, doesn't arrive gift wrapped from a digital assistant or even a human coach. It's something I had to dig out for myself, question by question and prompt by prompt.

And our job as the humans is to close that last mile and provide the real world experiences that AI can't get because they come after the knowledge cut off and it's also out there happening somewhere in the real world and AI is not in the real world, the physical world yet.

We think about AI as a productive technology, right? We value it for its ability to produce output and get things out of our, like just put stuff out. And what I found in my personal experience is that AI is just as powerful as a supportive technology.
compounding is the idea that every piece of feedback that you give to AI should feed back into the system to improve the next output.
My thesis on AI today is that education and access are going to matter more than they ever have before.

But the risk there is that value is going to compound to the small subset of people that happen to be early. And I just think that a much more compelling vision for an AI future is one where everyone is able to come along for the ride.
